LoloBuy customs declaration guide: describe and value a parcel accurately

A declaration should let customs identify what is inside, how many units are present and what was paid. It is not a tax-avoidance field or a guarantee of clearance. Build it from the order evidence before the parcel is packaged.

Editorial note: This independent guide is based on LoloBuy’s current public delivery agreement, declaration, restriction and customs materials, checked against current US Customs and Border Protection and European Commission consumer-import guidance on 18 October 2026. Destination rules and route terms can change; verify the live parcel page and the destination authority before dispatch.

What the declaration controls

LoloBuy’s delivery agreement says the platform uses the declared value entered by the buyer and can complete product name, quantity, unit price and related clearance information from the submitted product records. It also says the declared product name and quantity can be modified from the parcel details page before the parcel is packaged.

That makes the declaration review a real pre-dispatch decision. It is the point where several warehouse items become one customs-facing parcel record. A correct declaration should agree with the products selected for the parcel, the quantities visible in the warehouse, and the transaction evidence you can produce if a carrier or customs authority asks.

The declaration does not decide whether the parcel will be inspected, taxed, delayed, returned or released. Those outcomes depend on destination law, item eligibility, the chosen route, the accuracy of the data and the authority’s own assessment. Treat the form as evidence, not as a control panel for a preferred customs outcome.

Start with a parcel inventory

Before editing any customs field, write one line for every distinct product in the parcel. Record the ordinary item name, material or function when relevant, number of units, price paid per unit and total paid for that line. Link each line back to the LoloBuy order and warehouse item so the declaration can be reconciled with your account.

Do not use the seller’s promotional title as the customs description. A listing title may contain slogans, model codes, search keywords or brand references without saying what the object is. Customs needs an understandable commodity description. “Men’s cotton hooded sweatshirt” is more informative than “fashion top,” and “USB-C phone charging cable” is more informative than “digital accessory.”

For a mixed parcel, separate meaningfully different goods. Three cotton T-shirts can usually be one line with quantity three. A T-shirt, leather wallet and charging cable should not become “clothes and accessories.” The record should remain short, but it must not hide differences that affect identification, restrictions or classification.

Write a precise product description

US Customs and Border Protection currently instructs importers and brokers to use a clear, concise, plain-language description detailed enough to identify the commodity. Its published examples reject vague terms such as “accessories,” “general,” “sample” or a brand name by itself. European Commission guidance likewise says the declaration should correctly state the nature of the goods.

A useful description normally answers two questions: what is it, and what distinguishes its type? Include the material, intended use or product form when that detail matters. Examples include “women’s polyester shoulder bag,” “plastic display figurine,” “stainless-steel water bottle” and “wired computer mouse.” Do not add a material, brand or function that the listing and product evidence do not support.

A description must also be consistent with the physical parcel. Calling a pair of shoes “gift,” “sample” or “accessory” does not change what customs can see during examination. The goal is not to find the least specific wording accepted by the interface; it is to make the declaration understandable without a seller’s product page.

Use a supportable value

LoloBuy asks users to declare parcel value accurately. Current US CBP consumer guidance ties commercial-invoice value to the price paid for the goods, while the European Commission tells consumers to ensure the declaration correctly reflects the goods and their value. Keep the item order, payment record, seller price and any legitimate discount evidence together.

Do not copy the lowest price visible on a listing if you bought a more expensive option. Do not replace a paid price with a hoped-for tax threshold, and do not label a purchase as a free gift merely because the parcel is for personal use. If a discount changed the amount actually paid, preserve the transaction record that supports it.

Different authorities and routes can treat freight, insurance, discounts, coupons, packing costs or other additions differently when calculating customs value or taxable amount. The number entered in one LoloBuy field is not a universal tax calculation. Follow the live route instructions and the destination authority’s current valuation rules; ask the carrier or qualified customs professional when the treatment is unclear.

Match quantity, unit price and total

A declaration can look plausible while the arithmetic is wrong. For each line, confirm that quantity multiplied by unit value reconciles with the declared line total, subject to the interface’s rounding and currency rules. Then compare the combined value with the warehouse items actually selected.

Pay special attention to sets and multipacks. A seller unit may contain two socks, six replacement tips or a three-piece outfit. The declaration quantity should follow the live form’s unit convention, but the description should make the contents understandable. Do not count a set as one item in one field and six separate items in another without explaining the relationship.

If LoloBuy populated a name or quantity from the purchase record, review it rather than assuming automation resolved the customs meaning. The delivery agreement specifically allows changes before packaging. Use that window to correct vague translations, wrong unit counts or mismatches caused by consolidated orders.

Check route terms separately from declaration data

Some LoloBuy routes publish tax collection or declaration instructions tied to that specific line. Those terms can change and should be read on the live parcel screen at submission. A route that collects an estimated tax amount does not make an inaccurate description or value acceptable, and a route without an upfront tax line does not prove that no import charge will arise.

For European Union destinations, the European Commission currently states that goods dispatched from outside the EU require a customs declaration and may involve import VAT, customs duties, excise duties or clearance fees depending on the goods and transaction. For the United States, CBP rules and procedures depend on the commodity and entry circumstances. This guide deliberately does not publish a fixed duty-free threshold or rate table because these rules are destination-specific and can change.

Use the shipping route comparison guide to compare the live line’s eligibility, billing, tax wording, tracking and exception path. Do not select a route because an old forum post calls it “tax free” or “customs safe.”

A declaration cannot make a restricted item eligible

LoloBuy marks some warehouse items with a prohibited or restricted indicator and says route availability depends on item category. Batteries, liquids, powders, food, medicine, weapons and other regulated goods can face carrier, export or destination restrictions. The current route screen and applicable law—not the description you type—determine whether an item can travel.

Never rename a restricted product as a harmless category to make a route appear available. That creates a mismatch between the declaration, the order record and the physical item. LoloBuy’s delivery agreement places responsibility on the user to meet origin-country export and destination-country import requirements and warns that false declaration can create losses.

If a warehouse restriction looks incorrect, ask support to review the product classification with the logistics provider before paying for the parcel. Keep the full product specification available. A route exception or manual review should be documented in the account; it should not be inferred from a checkout button becoming clickable.

Verify recipient and document readiness

Customs clearance can require more than an item list. LoloBuy says it collects sender and recipient name, address, contact details and product information for waybills, transport, clearance and delivery. Depending on destination requirements, identity information may also be collected for verification and declaration.

Enter the recipient’s legal name and complete deliverable address in the format required by the route. Use a phone number and email that the recipient actively monitors. LoloBuy’s customs-inspection guidance says authorities may contact the recipient for an invoice or clearance information, especially when a parcel appears unusual, bulky, heavy or sensitive.

Keep invoices, order confirmations, payment evidence and a simple parcel inventory accessible until delivery is complete. If a customs request arrives, verify that it comes through the carrier, authority or official account channel and answer by the stated deadline. Do not send identity documents or payment information through an unverified message.

Final pre-packaging declaration check

  • Contents: every selected warehouse item appears once in the declaration inventory.
  • Description: each line identifies the actual commodity in plain language.
  • Quantity: units and set contents are consistent.
  • Value: the amount is supported by the transaction record, not a desired threshold.
  • Arithmetic: unit value, quantity and line totals reconcile.
  • Eligibility: the route accepts the real item category and destination.
  • Recipient: legal name, address and monitored contact details are correct.
  • Evidence: invoices, payment records and product details are saved.

Complete this review before packaging, while LoloBuy says product name and quantity can still be edited from parcel details. If the live interface does not allow a necessary correction, stop and ask support rather than sending data you know is wrong.

Conclusion: make the parcel record defensible

A strong LoloBuy customs declaration guide is not a list of tricks for avoiding tax. It is a method for producing a parcel record that agrees with the order, warehouse contents and payment evidence. Use specific product names, supportable values, consistent quantities and a route that accepts the actual goods.

No accurate declaration can promise zero tax, no inspection or automatic clearance. It can reduce avoidable mismatches and help you answer a legitimate information request.
